title: RAVEN: End-to-end Equivariant Robot Learning with RGB Cameras
claim: Raw camera images become geometric tokens that a symmetry-respecting transformer processes before a decoder outputs actions, end to end.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right, dotted module boxes with xN repeat loops
description: A wide left-to-right architecture diagram in three parts. On the left, two robot camera photos each pass through a ResNet trapezoid and a 'Projection to Rays' box. Extrinsics and intrinsics feed in from below, and a separate gripper state and pose branch goes through an MLP. The center is a dotted box labeled 'SE(3) Geometric Transformer' (xN). It holds a yellow panel, 'Feedforward in Local Frames', with rows of small pose-frame icons passing through blue MLP boxes. Next to it is a green panel, 'Attention in Global Frame', with curved dotted arrows linking the poses. On the right, a 'Relative Action Decoder' (xN) stacks causal attention, cross-attention and a feedforward layer, from bottom to top. It outputs end-effector pose icons, with a xK loop arrow. Pastel yellow, green and blue fills distinguish module types.
caption: The RAVEN Architecture: image observations are converted to geometric tokens by preprocessing with ResNet and assigning pose based on rays. The SE(3) Geometric Transformer efficiently processes the tokens with feedforward and geometric transform attention layers. Finally, an action decoder network refines relative end-effector motions with flow matching.
abstract: Recent work has shown that equivariant policy networks can achieve strong performance on robot manipulation tasks with limited human demonstrations. However, existing equivariant methods typically require structured inputs, such as 3D point clouds or top-down camera views, which prevents their use in low-cost setups or dynamic environments. In this work, we propose the first $\mathrm{SE}(3)$-equivariant policy learning framework that operates with only RGB image observations. The key insight is to treat image-based data as collections of rays that, unlike 2D pixels, transform under 3D roto-translations. Extensive experiments in both simulation with diverse robot configurations and real-world settings demonstrate that our method consistently surpasses strong baselines in both performance and efficiency.
